breakfast.name: Mekici (Fried Dough)
instructions: Dissolve yeast in warm water with sugar
Mix flour and salt, add yeast mixture
Knead into soft dough, rest 30 minutes
Pull off pieces and stretch thin
Deep fry until puffed and golden on both sides
Serve with crumbled feta and honey
breakfast.description: Puffy fried dough served with salty feta and sweet honey, a beloved Macedonian breakfast.

breakfast.name: Pastrmajlija (Macedonian Pizza)
instructions: Make dough with flour, yeast, water, salt; rise 1 hour
Season meat with paprika, salt, pepper
Shape dough into oval boat shape
Spread seasoned meat and onion over dough
Brush edges with beaten egg
Bake at 200°C for 25 minutes until golden
breakfast.description: A boat-shaped bread topped with seasoned diced meat, the pride of Štip.

breakfast.name: Maznik (Savory Pastry)
ingredients: Filo pastry (homemade rolled thin OR commercial)
Filling: cheese (white brined) and egg — or spinach and cheese — or leek and cheese
Sour milk or yoghurt for serving
instructions: Maznik is one of Macedonia's most important everyday pastries
Related to burek (widespread across the Balkans) but with Macedonian variations
The filling is layered with the filo — not rolled like a Serbian burek
Macedonian maznik with cheese and egg is the classic breakfast form
Brush each filo layer with butter or oil
Layer with filling: white brined cheese (similar to feta but Macedonian)
Bake at 200°C until golden and crispy
The pastry should shatter; the filling should be creamy-cheesy inside
Served with sour milk (kiselo mleko) poured over — the acidity cuts the fat
The sour milk accompaniment is distinctly Macedonian
Maznik for breakfast, lunch, or as a main — Macedonian pastry is a meal
breakfast.description: Macedonia's everyday savory pastry — filo layered with white brined cheese and egg, baked until the pastry shatters and the filling is creamy, served with kiselo mleko (sour milk) poured over. The sour milk accompaniment is distinctly Macedonian. Maznik is related to burek but arranged differently — layers not a roll. Made for breakfast, lunch, and all-day eating.

breakfast.name: Popara (Bread and Milk)
instructions: Popara is the poor man's breakfast of the Balkans — but beloved by all
Day-old bread that would otherwise go stale, revived in hot milk
Tear or cut bread into chunks in a deep bowl
Pour hot milk over — the bread softens immediately
Add butter and crumbled white cheese
The bread absorbs the milk — becomes soft, milky, slightly cheesy
Salt if needed (the cheese provides salt)
Popara represents Macedonian frugality — nothing is wasted
Old bread + the day's milk = a filling, warming breakfast
Popara is eaten across Serbia, Bulgaria, and North Macedonia
Each family has a slightly different version — the proportions vary
A comfort food that spans generations and social classes in the Balkans
breakfast.description: Macedonia's frugality breakfast — day-old bread torn into pieces, poured over with hot milk, topped with butter and crumbled brined white cheese. The bread absorbs the milk completely. Nothing is wasted — old bread becomes the next morning's breakfast. Popara is eaten across the Balkans (Serbia, Bulgaria, North Macedonia) with slight variations. Simple, filling, and genuinely comforting.

lunch.name: Tavče Gravče (Baked Beans)
instructions: Soak beans overnight, boil until tender
Sauté onions and peppers in oil
Mix beans with onions, peppers, paprika, and chili
Transfer to a clay pot (tava)
Bake at 180°C for 1 hour until top is crusty
Garnish with parsley and serve with bread
lunch.description: North Macedonia's national dish — slow-baked white beans in a clay pot with peppers and paprika.

lunch.name: Selsko Meso (Village Meat Stew)
instructions: Brown pork in oil in a clay pot
Add onions and cook until soft
Add mushrooms, peppers, and tomatoes
Season with paprika, salt, and pepper
Pour in wine and cover
Bake at 180°C for 45 minutes
lunch.description: A rustic clay-pot stew of pork, mushrooms, and vegetables cooked village-style.

lunch.name: Tavče Gravče (Baked Beans — National Dish)
ingredients: Tetovo beans (large white beans from the Tetovo region — the authentic bean)
instructions: Tavče gravče is North Macedonia's national dish — 'beans in a pan'
The Tetovo bean is specific — a large white bean grown in the Tetovo region
The long-cooked onion is the key technique — 30-40 minutes until caramelized and sweet
The onion sweetness and the bean creaminess together are the flavor
Soak beans overnight, boil separately until almost cooked
Make the sofrito: caramelize onion slowly in sunflower oil
Add sweet paprika, dried chili — the paprika colors the oil red-orange
Add beans to the caramelized onion — mix
Transfer to a clay pot (earthenware is traditional and important)
The clay pot regulates heat and adds subtle earthiness
Bake uncovered at 200°C for 45-60 minutes
The top beans form a skin — this skin is characteristic
Čubar (savory) is the herb — specific to Macedonian bean dishes
lunch.description: North Macedonia's national dish — large Tetovo white beans baked in a clay pot with long-caramelized onions, sweet red paprika, and čubar (Macedonian savory herb). The clay pot is not optional — it regulates heat and adds earthiness. The 30-40 minute onion caramelization is the foundation of the flavor. The top beans form a characteristic skin when baked. Tetovo beans are the specific variety; other beans are a substitute.

lunch.name: Shopska Salad (Macedonian Version)
ingredients: Green peppers (roasted and peeled, OR raw)
Sirene (white brined cheese — grated generously over the top)
instructions: Shopska salad is the region's most famous salad — contested between Bulgaria, Serbia, and North Macedonia
Each country claims it as their own — the debate is unresolved
The key: the sirene (white brined cheese) is grated and piled on top — not cubed, not crumbled — grated
The amount of cheese should be enough to cover the salad entirely in white
Slice tomatoes, cucumber, pepper, onion
Season with oil, vinegar, salt, parsley
Top with a very generous amount of finely grated sirene
The cheese-to-vegetable ratio should be nearly equal
North Macedonian version: often uses roasted peppers — this distinguishes it from Bulgarian
The roasted pepper adds a smoky, sweet depth the raw pepper lacks
Shopska is eaten throughout the summer when tomatoes are at their peak
lunch.description: North Macedonia's most famous salad — ripe tomatoes, cucumber, and roasted peppers (the Macedonian signature: roasted peppers rather than raw as in the Bulgarian version) topped with a snowfall of finely grated sirene (white brined cheese). The cheese must be grated, not cubed — the fine snow of cheese covers the salad completely. The debate between Bulgaria, North Macedonia, and Serbia over who owns shopska salad will never be settled.

dinner.name: Turli Tava (Mixed Vegetable and Meat Bake)
instructions: Layer vegetables and meat in a deep clay pot
Season each layer with paprika, salt, and pepper
Drizzle oil over the top
Add a cup of water
Cover and bake at 180°C for 75 minutes
Uncover for last 15 minutes to brown the top
dinner.description: A layered clay-pot bake of mixed meats and seasonal vegetables, a Macedonian Sunday tradition.

dinner.name: Ohridska Pastrmka (Ohrid Trout)
instructions: Score trout and insert garlic slices
Season with salt, pepper, and lemon juice
Stuff cavity with parsley and lemon slices
Drizzle with olive oil and wine
Bake at 190°C for 25 minutes
Serve with lemon wedges
dinner.description: Pan-roasted trout from Lake Ohrid, simply prepared to highlight its delicate flavor.

dinner.name: Ajvar (Roasted Red Pepper Relish)
ingredients: Red bell peppers (a large amount — they reduce dramatically)
Eggplant (for the smoky, soft version — optional)
instructions: Ajvar is North Macedonia's (and Serbia's) most important condiment — a national obsession
Made in autumn when red peppers are at their peak — September-October
The roasting: peppers are roasted over open flame or very high oven until charred
The char is essential — it is the smoke flavor of ajvar
Peel the charred skin — it slips off after steaming in a bag
The roasted peppers are soft, sweet, smoky
Blend or finely chop — the texture choice is personal
Cook in sunflower oil for 30-40 minutes — the water must evaporate
Ajvar reduces significantly — it takes many peppers to make a small amount
Season with salt, garlic, vinegar
Ajvar season in Macedonia: families gather, process hundreds of peppers
Jars of homemade ajvar are stored for winter — eaten with bread, meat, cheese
The best ajvar: smoky, sweet-savory, slightly sour
dinner.description: North Macedonia's autumn ritual condiment — hundreds of red peppers roasted until charred, peeled, and cooked down in oil into a thick, smoky-sweet-savory relish. Ajvar season (September-October) is a national event: families process hundreds of peppers together and jar ajvar for winter. The char from direct flame is the smoke flavor — it cannot be replicated with baking. Spread on bread, served with meat, or eaten with a spoon.

dinner.name: Pastrmajlija (Macedonian Pizza)
ingredients: Bread dough (leavened — the shape is oval, boat-like)
Eggs (cracked on top near the end of baking)
instructions: Pastrmajlija is a Macedonian specialty — named after 'pastrma' (cured dried beef)
The shape: oval, boat-like with raised edges — not round like pizza
The crust is a leavened bread dough, baked until crispy at the edges
The pastrma (cured beef) is layered on the dough
Bake in a very hot oven — traditionally a wood-fired oven
Near the end of baking: crack eggs directly onto the pastrmajlija
The eggs cook briefly — the yolk should still be slightly runny
The combination: crispy bread + salty cured beef + runny egg
Pastrmajlija is from Štip (a city in eastern Macedonia) — the Štip specialty
Macedonians from Štip consider themselves the custodians of the true pastrmajlija
Served cut into slices, eaten hot
dinner.description: North Macedonia's cured beef flatbread — an oval, boat-shaped leavened bread base covered with pastrma (dried cured beef) and baked in a wood-fired oven, with eggs cracked directly on top in the final minutes (yolk slightly runny). Pastrmajlija comes from Štip in eastern Macedonia; people from Štip are the self-appointed custodians of the true recipe. The crispy bread + salty dried beef + runny egg combination is the experience.

snacks.name: Ajvar (Roasted Pepper Spread)
instructions: Roast peppers and eggplants over open flame or in oven until charred
Peel and seed peppers, scoop out eggplant flesh
Chop finely or pulse in food processor
Cook in oil with garlic on low heat, stirring often, for 1 hour
Add vinegar and salt to taste
Cool and serve with crusty bread
snacks.description: A smoky roasted pepper and eggplant spread, made every autumn and jarred for the year.

snacks.name: Pita so Zelka (Cabbage Pastry)
ingredients: White cabbage (finely shredded, salted and squeezed dry)
Butter or oil for the layers
instructions: Pita (pastry) is a category in Macedonian cooking — there are dozens of varieties
Pita so zelka = pastry with cabbage — the wintertime pastry when cabbage is plentiful
Shred cabbage finely, salt, and SQUEEZE very dry — the water must be removed
Fry onion and the squeezed cabbage in oil until soft and sweet
Season with paprika, salt, pepper — the cabbage should be golden and fragrant
Roll out thin dough or use filo sheets
Layer with butter/oil, fill with cabbage
Roll or fold
Bake at 200°C until golden
The squeezed, cooked cabbage has a sweet, slightly caramelized flavor — not sour
Pita so zelka is the autumn and winter pastry — when cabbage is harvested
Eaten with yoghurt or sour cream
snacks.description: North Macedonia's winter cabbage pastry — white cabbage shredded, heavily salted and squeezed very dry (the moisture removal is essential), then fried with onion until sweet and golden, wrapped in thin buttered filo and baked. The squeezed-dry technique transforms bitter raw cabbage into sweet, savory filling. Eaten with yoghurt. Pita so zelka is the winter pastry when cabbage is the season's abundance.

snacks.name: Tarator (Cold Yoghurt Soup/Dip)
ingredients: Thick yoghurt (kiselo mleko — Macedonian sour milk yoghurt)
instructions: Tarator is shared across the Balkans and Turkey (cacık/tarator/tzatziki family)
The North Macedonian version: walnuts and generous dill distinguish it
Grate or dice cucumber very fine — salt and squeeze out water
Mix yoghurt with garlic (generous — this should be garlicky)
Add cucumber, dill, walnuts, olive oil, salt
Thin with cold water to desired consistency — from thick dip to cold soup
Refrigerate 30 minutes before serving — it improves as the flavors meld
The garlic in Macedonian tarator is pronounced — more than Greek tzatziki
The walnut is the Macedonian marker — adding richness and texture
Served cold — sometimes very cold with ice on hot days
Eaten as a soup, as a sauce, or as a dip with bread
snacks.description: North Macedonia's cold yoghurt preparation — thick kiselo mleko (Macedonian sour milk yoghurt) with cucumber, generous garlic, dill, and walnuts, thinned to a cold soup or kept thick as a dip. The walnuts distinguish the Macedonian version from Greek tzatziki or Turkish cacık. The garlic is pronounced — Macedonian tarator is seriously garlicky. Served ice-cold; sometimes literally served over ice.

snacks.name: Polneti Piperki (Stuffed Peppers, Macedonian Style)
instructions: Polneti piperki is one of North Macedonia's most beloved home dishes
Stuffed vegetables are central to Balkan cooking — peppers, tomatoes, zucchini all get stuffed
The rice-meat stuffing: raw rice mixed with fried onion-meat mixture
Raw rice is correct — it cooks inside the pepper, absorbing the meat juices
Cut the top off the pepper, remove seeds
Fill with the meat-rice mixture — not too full (the rice expands)
Replace the top — it acts as a lid
Place in a pot or baking dish
Cook in tomato sauce — the sauce steams the peppers
90 minutes: the peppers collapse and the rice cooks through
Serve with yoghurt on the side
Polneti piperki is the Sunday family meal in Macedonia
snacks.description: North Macedonia's Sunday family dish — bell peppers stuffed with raw rice and a beef-pork-onion mixture, cooked in tomato sauce until the peppers collapse and the rice absorbs the meat juices. The raw rice is correct: it cooks inside the pepper. Stuffed vegetables are central to Balkan cooking; the pepper version is Macedonia's most beloved. Served with yoghurt on the side.

desserts.name: Kadaif (Shredded Pastry with Walnuts)
instructions: Spread half the kadaif in a buttered pan
Layer chopped walnuts evenly
Cover with remaining kadaif, pour melted butter over
Bake at 180°C for 35 minutes until golden
Make syrup by boiling sugar and water with lemon juice
Pour cooled syrup over hot kadaif, let soak 2 hours
desserts.description: Crispy shredded pastry layered with walnuts and soaked in sweet syrup.

desserts.name: Tulumba (Fried Dough in Syrup)
instructions: Tulumba is an Ottoman pastry — found from Turkey to the Balkans to the Middle East
The name comes from the pump (tulumba) shape — the dough is extruded through a star nozzle
Make the choux-like dough: boil butter and water, add flour off heat, beat in eggs
The dough should be smooth and shiny — like choux pastry
Pipe through a star nozzle into hot oil — cut into 4-5cm pieces
The ridges from the star nozzle hold the syrup
Fry until golden all over — turning as they fry
While hot: transfer to cold sugar syrup
The hot pastry absorbs the cold syrup — the same technique as Greek loukoumades
Rest 30 minutes in the syrup
Tulumba should be sweet, crispy outside, slightly chewy inside, syrup-soaked
The Ottoman dessert legacy of Macedonia — tulumba at every pastry shop
desserts.description: North Macedonia's Ottoman fried pastry — choux-like dough extruded through a star nozzle and fried until golden, then soaked in cold sugar syrup (the hot-into-cold technique drives syrup deep into the pastry). The ridges from the star nozzle hold the syrup. Tulumba is the Ottoman dessert legacy shared from Turkey through the Balkans; every Macedonian pastry shop has them. Sweet, sticky, crispy outside, slightly chewy inside.

desserts.name: Sutlijaš (Baked Rice Pudding)
instructions: Sutlijaš is North Macedonia's baked rice pudding — from the Turkish sütlaç
An Ottoman legacy dessert — sütlaç made the journey from Istanbul to Macedonia
Simmer rice in milk with sugar and vanilla — stir regularly
When mostly thick, pour into individual earthenware dishes or one large dish
Bake at 180°C for 20-30 minutes — a golden-brown skin forms on top
The skin is the most prized part
Dust with cinnamon
The flavor: creamy, milky, gently sweet, very vanilla-forward
The earthenware dish absorbs heat evenly — important for the skin formation
Sutlijaš is Macedonia's comfort dessert — made at home and at traditional restaurants
The Ottoman dessert legacy is deep in Macedonian cooking — centuries of shared food culture
desserts.description: North Macedonia's Ottoman baked rice pudding — rice simmered in milk until thick, poured into earthenware and baked until a golden-brown skin forms on top. The skin is the most prized part. From the Turkish sütlaç (milk pudding), a direct Ottoman culinary legacy. The earthenware dish is traditional and functional — it absorbs heat evenly for the proper skin. Macedonia's most homely comfort dessert.

drinks.name: Boza (Fermented Grain Drink)
instructions: Cook millet flour in water, stirring constantly, for 30 minutes
Cool to room temperature
Stir in sugar and yeast
Cover and ferment at room temperature for 24-48 hours
Strain through cheesecloth and refrigerate
Serve cold with a sprinkle of cinnamon
drinks.description: A thick, tangy fermented millet drink enjoyed chilled, with centuries of Balkan tradition.

drinks.name: Rakija (Grape Brandy)
instructions: Crush grapes and place in a fermentation vessel
Let ferment naturally for 3-4 weeks, stirring daily
Transfer fermented mash to a copper still
Distill slowly, collecting the middle run
Discard the first and last portions
Age in oak barrel or bottle immediately
drinks.description: A potent grape brandy distilled at home, the ritual spirit of every Macedonian celebration.

drinks.name: Macedonian Red Wine (Vranec / Temjanika)
ingredients: Macedonian red wine: Vranec (indigenous red grape)
instructions: Macedonia has produced wine since at least 2000 BCE — one of the world's oldest wine regions
The Tikveš Valley is the heartland of Macedonian wine
Vranec is the most important indigenous red grape — 'the black stallion'
Deep purple-red, full-bodied, high tannin, complex — a serious red wine
In the 1970s-80s, Yugoslav Macedonia was producing 25% of all Yugoslav wine
Macedonian wine was foundational to British and German cheap wine supply — blended anonymously
After independence (1991), Macedonia began establishing its own wine identity
Temjanika: an aromatic white with a strong floral, muscat character
Both Vranec and Temjanika are specifically Macedonian contributions to the wine world
Served at all Macedonian celebrations and family meals
The wine culture of the Tikveš region is ancient and modern simultaneously
drinks.description: North Macedonia's wine heritage — Vranec (indigenous deep purple-red grape, 'the black stallion') and Temjanika (aromatic white, muscat-floral). Macedonia's Tikveš Valley has produced wine since 2000 BCE. In the Yugoslav era, Macedonian wine was 25% of all Yugoslav production — much of it blended anonymously into British and German cheap wine. Since 1991 independence, Vranec and Temjanika are establishing Macedonia's own wine identity.
